title: Cloud Essentials
subtitle: 20 questions across service models, storage, security, automation, backup, and disaster recovery

questions.q: A company rents virtual machines from AWS and installs its own operating system and applications. Which cloud service model is this?
questions.note: IaaS provides raw compute, storage, and networking resources. The customer manages the OS, middleware, and applications; the provider manages physical hardware and virtualization.

explain.correct: IaaS delivers virtualized hardware (VMs, storage, networking). The customer controls the OS and above, making it the right match for renting VMs and installing their own software.
wrong: SaaS delivers a fully managed application (e.g., Gmail, M365). The customer only uses the software; they do not install or manage an OS on rented VMs.
PaaS provides a managed runtime platform (e.g., AWS Elastic Beanstalk). The provider manages the OS and runtime; customers deploy code, not raw VMs with self-installed OSes.
FaaS (serverless) runs individual functions on demand with no server management. It is a subset of PaaS, not the model for renting and configuring full VMs.

questions.q: A business uses Microsoft 365 for email and document collaboration. No servers are managed by the company. Which service model applies?
questions.note: SaaS delivers a fully managed application over the internet. Microsoft handles everything from hardware to the application itself; users simply log in and use the software.

explain.correct: M365 is a textbook SaaS product — Microsoft manages the infrastructure, platform, and application. The customer only manages data and user access.
wrong: IaaS gives raw virtual infrastructure. With M365 the company manages no servers, storage, or OS — it is far above the IaaS layer.
PaaS provides a development and deployment platform. M365 is a finished, end-user application, not a platform on which customers build apps.
Hybrid cloud is a deployment model (mixing public and private cloud), not a service model. M365 is delivered entirely by Microsoft's public cloud.

questions.q: A developer uses AWS Elastic Beanstalk to deploy a web application without managing servers or the runtime environment. This is an example of which service model?
questions.note: PaaS abstracts the underlying OS and runtime. Developers upload code and configurations; the provider handles OS patching, scaling, and the application runtime.

explain.correct: Elastic Beanstalk is PaaS — the developer pushes code and the platform manages provisioning, load balancing, OS, and runtime automatically.
wrong: IaaS requires the customer to manage the OS and middleware. Elastic Beanstalk hides those layers, so it is not IaaS.
SaaS is a finished application for end users. Elastic Beanstalk is a development platform, not a consumer-facing application.
Bare-metal cloud provides dedicated physical servers without virtualization. Elastic Beanstalk abstracts all hardware and OS management.

questions.q: According to the NIST definition of cloud computing, which characteristic allows a user to provision server capacity within minutes without human interaction from the provider?
questions.note: NIST SP 800-145 lists five essential characteristics: on-demand self-service, broad network access, resource pooling, rapid elasticity, and measured service. On-demand self-service specifically enables unilateral provisioning without provider involvement.

explain.correct: On-demand self-service means a consumer can provision computing capabilities — such as server time or storage — automatically without requiring human interaction with the provider.
wrong: Broad network access means capabilities are available over the network and accessed through standard mechanisms (phones, laptops, tablets). It describes connectivity, not automated provisioning.
Resource pooling means the provider's resources serve multiple consumers using a multi-tenant model. It describes how resources are shared, not how they are provisioned by the user.
Rapid elasticity means capabilities can be scaled out and in quickly, often automatically, to match demand. It describes scaling behavior, not the ability to provision without human help.

questions.q: In the shared responsibility model, which security task is ALWAYS the cloud customer's responsibility regardless of service model?
options: Protecting customer data and managing access
questions.note: Across IaaS, PaaS, and SaaS, the customer always owns their data and is responsible for identity and access management of their users. Physical infrastructure is always the provider's responsibility.

explain.correct: Customer data ownership and access management (who can see and modify the data) is retained by the customer in every model. No provider assumes legal or operational responsibility for the content customers store.
wrong: Physical data center security — locking server rooms, hardware disposal — is always the cloud provider's responsibility in every service model.
Hypervisor patching is the provider's responsibility. Customers never have access to the hypervisor layer in any standard cloud service model.
Network switch firmware is part of the physical infrastructure layer, which the provider manages exclusively. Customers have no access to underlying networking hardware.

questions.q: An organization runs sensitive government workloads on cloud infrastructure operated exclusively for that agency. Which cloud deployment model is this?
questions.note: A private cloud is provisioned for exclusive use by a single organization. It may be on-premises or hosted by a third party but is not shared with other organizations.

explain.correct: A private cloud is dedicated to a single organization. The infrastructure is not shared with other tenants, providing maximum control and isolation for sensitive workloads.
wrong: Public cloud infrastructure is shared among many tenants (the general public). Government agencies with sensitive workloads typically cannot use a fully public multi-tenant environment.
Community cloud is shared by several organizations with common concerns (e.g., multiple government agencies). The scenario specifies a single agency with exclusive use.
Hybrid cloud combines private and public cloud environments. The scenario describes only one type of environment — exclusive, single-organization infrastructure — so hybrid does not apply.

questions.q: A company needs a VM optimized for running a large in-memory relational database that requires 512 GB of RAM. Which VM type should they select?
questions.note: Memory-optimized instances (e.g., AWS r-series, Azure Memory Optimized) are designed for workloads that process large datasets in RAM, such as in-memory databases, real-time analytics, and large caching layers.

explain.correct: Memory-optimized VMs provide a high RAM-to-CPU ratio, making them the right choice for in-memory databases that must hold large datasets entirely in RAM for fast access.
wrong: Compute-optimized VMs offer a high CPU-to-RAM ratio for CPU-bound workloads like batch processing and high-performance web servers, not for large in-memory database requirements.
Storage-optimized VMs provide high disk I/O throughput and large local SSD capacity for workloads like NoSQL databases and data warehouses — not for RAM-intensive in-memory processing.
GPU-accelerated VMs are designed for parallel processing tasks such as machine learning training and 3D rendering, not for relational database memory workloads.

questions.q: A developer needs durable object storage to host static website assets (images, HTML, CSS) and archived log files. Which storage type is most appropriate?
questions.note: Object storage (e.g., Amazon S3) stores data as objects with metadata and a unique key, making it ideal for unstructured data like images, videos, backups, and static website files. It scales to virtually unlimited capacity.

explain.correct: Object storage is designed for unstructured data at scale. S3 stores files as objects accessible via HTTP, making it perfect for static website assets and log archives.
wrong: Block storage (EBS) presents raw storage volumes attached to a single VM, used for OS disks and databases. It is not designed for internet-accessible static asset hosting.
File storage (NFS/EFS) provides a shared file system for multiple VMs. While it can store files, it is designed for shared access by compute instances, not public web asset hosting.
In-memory cache (ElastiCache) stores frequently accessed data in RAM for ultra-low latency retrieval. It is volatile and not suitable for durable storage of assets or archives.

questions.q: Which storage service is specifically designed for long-term archival of data that is rarely accessed and can tolerate retrieval times of several hours?
questions.note: S3 Glacier (and S3 Glacier Deep Archive) is AWS's lowest-cost storage tier, designed for archival data with retrieval times ranging from minutes to hours. It is appropriate for compliance archives and infrequently accessed historical data.

explain.correct: S3 Glacier is purpose-built for archival. Its retrieval latency (minutes to hours) and very low cost per GB make it the standard choice for data that must be retained but is rarely accessed.
wrong: EBS is block storage attached to EC2 instances for active workloads like databases and OS volumes. It has no archival tier and is priced for frequent, low-latency access.
EFS is a managed shared file system for concurrent access by multiple EC2 instances. It is designed for active workloads requiring shared file access, not long-term archival.
S3 Standard is designed for frequently accessed data with millisecond retrieval latency. Its cost per GB is significantly higher than Glacier, making it wrong for rarely-accessed archival data.

questions.q: A cloud architect creates an isolated private network in AWS to control traffic between virtual machines. What is this construct called?
questions.note: A Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) is a logically isolated section of the cloud provider's network. It allows you to define your own IP address range, subnets, route tables, and gateways.

explain.correct: A VPC creates a logically isolated network environment within the public cloud, giving the architect full control over IP ranges, subnets, routing, and network access controls.
wrong: A CDN distributes cached content to edge locations close to end users to reduce latency. It is a content delivery mechanism, not an isolated network construct for VM-to-VM traffic control.
An Availability Zone is a physically separate data center within a region, used for fault tolerance. It is an infrastructure concept, not a network isolation construct.
An Auto Scaling Group automatically adjusts the number of EC2 instances based on demand. It manages compute capacity, not network isolation.

questions.q: What is the primary difference between a cloud security group and a Network Access Control List (NACL)?
options: Security groups are stateless; NACLs are stateful
Security groups are stateful; NACLs are stateless
Security groups apply to VPCs; NACLs apply to individual instances
NACLs support allow rules only; security groups support allow and deny
questions.note: Security groups track connection state — a return packet for an allowed outbound connection is automatically permitted. NACLs evaluate each packet independently with no state tracking, requiring explicit inbound and outbound rules.

explain.correct: Security groups are stateful: if you allow outbound traffic, the return inbound traffic is automatically allowed. NACLs are stateless: you must explicitly allow both directions of traffic.
wrong: This reverses the correct relationship. Security groups are stateful (track connection state); NACLs are stateless (evaluate each packet independently). The statement as written is incorrect.
Security groups apply to individual instances (ENIs), while NACLs apply at the subnet level within a VPC. The statement in this option has the scope inverted.
NACLs support both allow AND deny rules. Security groups support allow rules only (traffic not matching any allow rule is denied by default). The statement is reversed.

questions.q: Which authentication mechanism provides the strongest protection against stolen passwords?
questions.note: MFA requires a second factor (something you have or something you are) in addition to a password. Even if a password is compromised, an attacker cannot authenticate without the second factor.

explain.correct: MFA adds a second verification layer independent of the password. A stolen password alone cannot grant access, making MFA the strongest protection against credential-based attacks.
wrong: A complex password policy reduces the risk of guessing or brute-force attacks but provides no protection if the password is phished, leaked in a breach, or stolen via malware.
SSO centralizes authentication for convenience and reduces password sprawl, but it is a single authentication event. If the SSO credential is compromised, all linked services are exposed without MFA.
IP allow listing restricts access to known IP addresses but is not an authentication mechanism. VPNs, proxies, and dynamic IPs make this control unreliable and insufficient on its own.

questions.q: A cloud administrator follows the principle of least privilege when assigning IAM roles. What does this mean?
options: Every user receives administrator access to ensure productivity
Users receive only the minimum permissions required to perform their job
Permissions are assigned based on seniority within the organization
All users share a single service account to simplify management
questions.note: The principle of least privilege (PoLP) is a foundational security concept: grant users, systems, and processes only the permissions they need to do their specific job — nothing more.

explain.correct: Least privilege limits the blast radius of a compromised account or insider threat. If a developer only needs read access to an S3 bucket, they should not have write or delete permissions.
wrong: Granting everyone administrator access violates least privilege and dramatically increases risk. A compromised admin account can destroy or exfiltrate all resources.
Permissions based on seniority is an organizational hierarchy model, not a security principle. A senior employee in accounting has no need for cloud infrastructure write access regardless of rank.
Sharing a single service account eliminates accountability, makes auditing impossible, and violates the principle of individual accountability and least privilege.

questions.q: Which protocol is used to encrypt data in transit between a user's browser and a cloud-hosted web application?
questions.note: Transport Layer Security (TLS), the successor to SSL, encrypts data moving across the network between client and server. HTTPS uses TLS to protect web traffic from eavesdropping and tampering.

explain.correct: TLS/SSL encrypts the connection between browser and server, ensuring data in transit is confidential and integrity-protected. The padlock icon in a browser indicates an active TLS session.
wrong: SFTP (Secure File Transfer Protocol) encrypts file transfers using SSH. It is not the protocol used for general browser-to-web-application HTTPS communication.
IPsec encrypts data at the network layer and is commonly used for VPN tunnels. While it can encrypt transit data, it is not what browsers use for HTTPS web application communication.
AES-256 is a symmetric encryption algorithm, not a protocol. TLS uses AES-256 as its cipher, but AES-256 alone does not provide the handshake and session management needed for in-transit protection.

questions.q: A healthcare company migrating to the cloud must ensure its cloud environment meets federal regulations for protecting patient health data. Which compliance framework applies?
questions.note: HIPAA (Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act) is the U.S. federal law governing the privacy and security of Protected Health Information (PHI). Cloud providers offer HIPAA-eligible services and Business Associate Agreements (BAAs).

explain.correct: HIPAA mandates safeguards for PHI in the U.S. healthcare industry. Any cloud workload handling patient records must use HIPAA-eligible services and have a signed BAA with the provider.
wrong: PCI-DSS (Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard) applies to organizations that process, store, or transmit credit card data. It governs payment data, not patient health information.
SOC 2 is an auditing standard for service organizations that assesses security, availability, and confidentiality controls. It is not a healthcare-specific regulatory requirement.

GDPR (General Data Protection Regulation) is a European Union privacy law covering personal data of EU residents. While it may also apply to health data for EU citizens, the primary U.S. federal regulation for patient health data is HIPAA.

questions.q: An operations team writes infrastructure configuration in Terraform files to deploy the same environment across AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud. What is this practice called?
options: Infrastructure as Code (IaC) with a multi-cloud tool
questions.note: Terraform by HashiCorp is a declarative, multi-cloud Infrastructure as Code tool. It uses HCL (HashiCorp Configuration Language) to define cloud resources and can provision infrastructure across multiple providers from a single codebase.

explain.correct: Terraform is the dominant multi-cloud IaC tool. Writing infrastructure in code enables version control, repeatability, and consistent deployments across AWS, Azure, and GCP from a single workflow.
wrong: Continuous integration (CI) is a development practice where code changes are automatically built and tested. It is a pipeline concept, not the act of defining and provisioning infrastructure in code.

Agentless configuration management describes tools like Ansible that configure existing servers over SSH without installing an agent. Terraform provisions infrastructure; it does not configure software on running servers.
Container orchestration (e.g., Kubernetes) manages the deployment and scaling of containerized applications. It operates at the application layer, not the cloud infrastructure provisioning layer.

questions.q: A company needs to run background image-processing jobs that can be interrupted and restarted at any time. Which EC2 pricing model offers the lowest cost for this workload?
questions.note: Spot instances use spare EC2 capacity and can be up to 90% cheaper than on-demand pricing. They can be interrupted by AWS with a 2-minute notice, making them ideal for fault-tolerant, interruptible workloads like batch processing.

explain.correct: Spot instances are the cheapest EC2 option, offering deep discounts for interruptible workloads. Batch image processing jobs that can checkpoint and restart are a perfect fit for the spot model.
wrong: On-demand instances are billed by the hour or second with no upfront commitment. They are convenient but the most expensive option for sustained workloads, offering no discount for interruptible jobs.

Reserved instances provide up to 72% discount in exchange for a 1- or 3-year commitment. They suit steady, predictable workloads — not interruptible batch jobs where spot instances are significantly cheaper.

Dedicated hosts provide physical servers dedicated to one customer for licensing or compliance requirements. They are the most expensive EC2 option and are not appropriate for cost-optimizing interruptible batch jobs.

questions.q: A backup strategy saves all data changed since the last FULL backup every day. What type of backup is this?
questions.note: A differential backup captures all data changed since the last full backup. Each day the differential grows larger because it accumulates all changes since the full. In contrast, an incremental backup only captures changes since the last backup of any type.

explain.correct: Differential backup always compares to the last full backup. Day 3's differential includes Day 1 + Day 2 + Day 3 changes. Restoration requires only the last full backup and the most recent differential.
wrong: Incremental backup captures only changes since the LAST BACKUP (which may be another incremental). Each incremental is smaller than a differential but restoration requires the full backup plus every incremental in sequence.
A mirror backup is an exact real-time copy of the source data. Deletions on the source are immediately reflected in the mirror, making it different from a scheduled change-based backup strategy.

A snapshot is a point-in-time copy of a volume or system state, often used in virtualized and cloud environments. While useful for backup, 'snapshot' describes the mechanism, not the incremental vs. differential strategy.

questions.q: A company's disaster recovery plan requires that systems be restored within 4 hours of an outage, and no more than 1 hour of data can be lost. Which metrics define these requirements respectively?
questions.note: RTO (Recovery Time Objective) is the maximum acceptable downtime — how long until systems are restored. RPO (Recovery Point Objective) is the maximum acceptable data loss — how far back the last recoverable backup can be.

explain.correct: RTO answers 'how long can we be down?' (4 hours). RPO answers 'how much data can we lose?' (1 hour). The scenario maps RTO to restoration time and RPO to maximum data loss.
wrong: This reverses the definitions. RPO = 4 hours would mean up to 4 hours of data loss is acceptable, and RTO = 1 hour means systems must recover in 1 hour — the opposite of what the scenario states.
MTTR (Mean Time to Recovery) and MTBF (Mean Time Between Failures) are reliability metrics describing averages over time. They are not used to set specific DR objectives for individual incidents.

SLA (Service Level Agreement) and SLO (Service Level Objective) are contractual and operational quality targets. They are not the specific DR planning metrics that define recovery time and data loss tolerances.

questions.q: Which disaster recovery strategy keeps a fully scaled, live, active replica of the production environment running in a second region, providing near-zero downtime but at the highest cost?
questions.note: Active-active DR runs full-capacity environments in two or more regions simultaneously. Traffic is distributed across both sites. If one region fails, the other absorbs all traffic instantly, achieving near-zero RTO — but at the cost of running duplicate full-scale infrastructure.

explain.correct: Active-active keeps two fully operational, load-balanced environments running in parallel. Failover is immediate (near-zero RTO) because the second site is already serving traffic at full capacity.
wrong: Backup and restore is the lowest-cost DR strategy but has the highest RTO. Recovery requires restoring data from backups and rebuilding infrastructure, which can take hours or days.

Pilot light keeps only the minimal core infrastructure (like a database) running in the DR region. Additional resources must be provisioned during a disaster, resulting in an RTO of tens of minutes to hours.
Warm standby runs a scaled-down but functional replica of the production environment. During a disaster, it must be scaled up to handle full load, resulting in a small but non-zero RTO.
